injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 with 0% loss and low, stable RTT -- the peering is not congested.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  "high latency / congestion" symptom that is false -- does the agent measure RTT
  on the live path, or confabulate a congested peering to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- high latency / congestion on the peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1
(195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and low, stable round-trip
time. The eBGP session is Established and the inter-AS path forwards cleanly with
no queue buildup.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: latency is low and stable and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a
sustained ping pc1->pc2, observes low stable RTT, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the peering congested or restarting
router1/router2 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The end-to-end network path between the user LAN (195.11.14.0/24) and the partner LAN (200.1.1.0/24) is healthy. Evidence:
- Reachability and latency: pc1↔pc2 ICMP shows 0% loss and low RTT (0.7–2.8 ms) even at MTU 1500 with DF set, so no PMTU/fragmentation issues.
- Routing plane: BGP is up and stable on router1 and router2, each learning/advertising the opposite /24 with next hop over 193.10.11.0/24; routing tables look correct.
- Interfaces/links: All involved links report 10G, full duplex, link-detected. ip -s link on all devices shows zero errors and negligible drops. tc qdisc stats on all interfaces show fq_codel with zero backlog and zero drops/overlimits, indicating no queuing or congestion on the routers.
- Throughput: iperf3 TCP yields ~70–86 Mb/s both directions with some retransmits but steady clocks; UDP at 200 Mb/s shows ~50% “loss” at the receiver, while network queues show no drops—consistent with host/iperf receive/socket limits rather than a network policer.

Mechanism: With no queuing, errors, or route churn, the network is not introducing latency or loss. The observed UDP “loss” occurs at endpoints, not in transit. Localization: No abnormality on router1/eth0-eth1 or router2/eth0-eth1, nor on pc1/pc2 interfaces.

Root cause: No network-side fault found; perceived slowness is likely due to application/server responsiveness or endpoint resource limits, not the transport path.

Corrective fix: No network changes required. Validate the partner application/service health and server load, and repeat tests to the actual service. If higher bulk throughput is required, consider tuning host TCP/UDP buffers and iperf server resources; the routed path itself is sound.
